21200-the-letters-of-cicero-volume-1-the:
Evelyn S. Shuckburgh translated the whole surviving correspondence of Cicero into English, arranged in time order, for this four-volume edition published in London in 1899. Volume One covers the years 68 to 52 BC. Shuckburgh had also translated Polybius and written a history of Rome.

Cicero's letters, kept by his freedman Tiro, begin only in Cicero's thirty-ninth year, so no boyhood letters survive. What remains deals closely with daily politics: elections, trials, exile, and family matters. The letters let readers watch the late Roman Republic through the eyes of its greatest speaker, writing frankly to friends like Atticus about each crisis.
22778-the-remarkable-adventures-of-an-ol:
The Remarkable Adventures of an Old Woman and Her Pig is an ancient nursery tale in verse. Its cumulative story follows a dame whose pig will not jump over the stile. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Every child once knew the chain: the dog must bite the pig, the stick must beat the dog, and so on down the line.

The dame, out of patience, cries in a fright to a passing dog. Pray, give Piggy a bite, she begs, and compel him over the stile. Or here I may stay till midnight. Mr. Bow-wow, of course, hears the request, but silently stands without saying a word. Her threats of being even with him only lengthen the chain. Such tales taught rhythm, memory, and comic exasperation to the youngest readers.

france-and-england-in-north-america-part: Parkman's Pioneers of France in the New World opens his monumental history. Hardy French explorers brave the vast wilderness of North America. Champlain, La Salle, and their bold rivals come alive. Great history written like high epic adventure.

govdocs-archive_org-nsia-PressResearchIn:
A newspaper article reports on Press Research Inc., a service that sold interpretive reports to subscriber newspapers. One report caused a fight: a 45,000-word study of Thomas Dewey, the Republican candidate, which Democrats bought. The article also covers reports that booklets attacking Dewey were being burned.

Interpretive-report services sold analysis to editors who wanted background with a slant measured to order. A 45,000-word report bought by one party, and booklets burned by someone, made the service itself the story. The article preserves the episode's elements: the company, the report's size, the buyers, and the burnings. It is a look at the information trade inside a presidential campaign of the 1940s.
nasa-tm-19670030533-certain-general-patt:
B. A. Kolachev, V. A. Livanov, N. Ya. Gusel'nikov, and A. A. Bukhanova wrote this study in Russian, published in 1965. It seeks general patterns in hydrogen brittleness in two titanium alloys, VT3-1 and VT15. Hydrogen can sneak into titanium and make it crack like glass. The translation was issued at Redstone Arsenal in July 1967.

Brittleness in VT3-1, they show, develops most strongly below room temperature and at low strain rates. Beta alloys like VT15 are also prone below room temperature, in a narrow range and only when strained slowly. The authors trace the cause to processes in the beta phase during deformation. Both alloys, they conclude, turn brittle in much the same manner.
nasa-tm-19700025196-preliminary-lunar-or:
E. C. Howell, C. R. Hunt, and V. W. Simmons of the TRW Systems Group wrote this internal note for the Manned Spacecraft Center. It is dated February 21, 1969. It gives a first lunar orbit attitude sequence for Mission F, the Apollo 10 flight, which rehearsed the landing without touching down.

The sequence walks revolution by revolution through the spacecraft's time in lunar orbit. Steps cover the crew's sleep period, then undocking and the descent orbit insertion burn. Later steps run from that burn's cutoff through the phasing, insertion, and circularization burns. Each step is paired with figures, so planners could see the planned pointing at every stage.
nasa-tm-19700025414-evaluation-of-manned:
Tommie L. Wheeler and Edgar A. Dalie of the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston wrote this evaluation of prelaunch checkout. For three or four years, center staff had been bringing the ACE-S/C checkout system into Apollo work. That system ran the tests of the command, service, and lunar modules before launch.

Day-to-day use taught the staff where the system fell short. They fixed running problems and drew up design changes as they went. The paper judges how well the system meets the true test needs of the spacecraft. Checkout quality decides whether faults are caught on the ground, where they can still be fixed.
nasa-tm-19710002734-overall-performance-:
Carl Weigel Jr., Edward R. Tysl, and Calvin L. Ball of the Lewis Research Center wrote this report in November 1970. It gives the overall performance of a small centrifugal compressor running on argon gas. The wheel carries sweptback blades and serves gas loop power systems.

Performance is charted against the weight of gas flowing through the machine. At the design flow and tip speed, the compressor reached the pressure rise and efficiency the abstract records. The best efficiency at design speed came at a somewhat lower flow. Compressors of this size drive the working gas around closed Brayton power loops for space.
nasa-tm-19710023020-atlas-centaur-ac-19-:
Lewis Research Center staff reviewed two Atlas Centaur launches in this July 1971 memorandum, NASA TM X-2278. Vehicles AC-19 and AC-20 carried the Mariner Mars probes of 1969. Both used a direct, single burn ascent. AC-20 placed Mariner VI on its path, and AC-19 placed Mariner VII. The launches took place in the first quarter of 1969.

Mariner VI flew past Mars on an equatorial pass on July 31, 1969. Five days later, Mariner VII passed over the planet's south pole. The report discusses how each launch vehicle performed in flight. Such postflight reviews confirmed the Atlas Centaur as a reliable planetary launcher. They also fed lessons into later missions.
nasa-tm-19720004682-ionospheric-nf-sub-h:
A NASA preprint numbered X-621-71-214 studies echoes that the Alouette 2 satellite picked up in the upper air. The scan leaves its author names unreadable. The echoes sat near harmonics of the electron gyro rate, the rate at which electrons circle in Earth's field. Their frequencies sat slightly off the values that field models predicted.

Plasma wave effects, the paper reports, can explain the shifts in a consistent way. Two offsets also play a part. One is a small positive offset in the sounder transmitter's own frequency. The other is a small negative offset in Earth's field, set against the model field. Large positive shifts once blamed on the echoes themselves can instead come from the instrument offset. The field offset fits with magnetic readings taken by the OGO 3 and OGO 5 satellites at higher altitudes.
podcast-dannyjones-R3I2yU1mfNc:
Historian Rebecca Lemov wrote a history of brainwashing research and now studies the sciences of mind control at Harvard. On Danny Jones's podcast, she explains why she fears MK-Ultra, the CIA's notorious mind control program, is still active in modern forms, carried on by new institutions with better tools.

Lemov's authority is archival; she has read the program's surviving records and interviewed its world. She connects the Cold War experiments to today's data-driven influence systems with a scholar's care for the differences. Jones draws out the continuities that alarm her. The episode offers the strongest historically grounded version of a popular fear, from the person best qualified to judge the original. Listeners can weigh her evidence for survival of the program's spirit against the official story of its burial.
podcast-dannyjones-XyVKTJYxmnc:
George Howard joins Danny Jones to talk about the search for Sodom and Gomorrah, the two cities destroyed in the Bible. The episode title says scholars of the Bible have found the lost city. Howard speaks for the dig and its claims.

Howard lays out the site, the layer of ash and ruin, and why his team links it to the Bible story. He also deals with the doubts raised by other scholars who place the cities elsewhere. Jones walks through the finds one by one. Listeners get a field report from a dig that claims to match one of the most famous tales in scripture.
podcast-dannyjones-vZZqv0SYAnc:
Historian John Newman returns to Danny Jones with newly freed JFK files he says prove a Russian mole sat inside the CIA. Newman has read the case files for decades. The mole claim goes to the heart of Cold War spy lore.

Newman walks through the new pages and the names they clear or cloud. He argues the mole hunt tore the agency in half and still shapes how it acts. Jones asks what the files at last settle. Listeners who love spy craft get a dense, rich talk. The library holds it as an archive record of his reading.
podcast-tuckercarlson-DE2AVar-XNc:
Maine reporter Steve Robinson joins Tucker Carlson to expose a drug network in his state. Carlson calls him one of the last independent journalists in Maine. Their film on the case is called High Crimes.

Robinson says Chinese cartels took over drug trade in the rural Northeast. He blames ignored border laws and failed local duty. The title also charges that politicians cover the trade up. Carlson presents the story as proof of a wider takeover. Listeners get a local reporter's case that stunned even a veteran host. The film extends the same case on screen.
podcast-tuckercarlson-LhqSdfw-enc:
Country star John Rich and comedian Russell Brand join Tucker Carlson together, and the announced theme is Christianity as the new counterculture: faith as rebellion in a secular age. The second thread is an accusation, that the neoconservatives are lying America into a third world war.

Rich brings the Nashville plain-spokenness his fans expect, Brand the theatrical sermonizing of his recent years, and Carlson the host's frame that joins them. All three men have remade themselves as faith-forward populists, and the episode functions as a summit of that tendency. War skepticism and revival preaching blend into one message: the old order lies, the old faith saves. Listeners get the movement's mood at full volume, from three of its most recognizable voices, arguing in friendly unison.

the-papers-and-writings-of-abraham-linco:
Volume Three of The Papers and Writings of Abraham Lincoln, in the Constitutional Edition edited by Arthur Brooks Lapsley, is given to the Lincoln-Douglas debates. It opens with Lincoln's speech at Springfield on June 17, 1858, at the close of the Republican State Convention that named him for the United States Senate. Douglas was not present.

Lincoln argues that slavery agitation will not cease until a crisis is reached and passed. A house divided against itself cannot stand, he says. The government cannot endure permanently half slave and half free. It will become all one thing or all the other. He then traces the Nebraska doctrine and the Dred Scott decision as parts of one legal machine.

Volume Four of The Papers and Writings of Abraham Lincoln, in the Constitutional Edition edited by Arthur Brooks Lapsley, continues the Lincoln-Douglas debates. The pages present open with the fourth debate, at Charleston on September 18, 1858. Lincoln begins by asking the huge crowd for silence so his words can be heard.

He then answers a question put to him at his hotel that day. In the speech as printed, Lincoln states that he is not in favor of social and political equality between the white and black races, nor of negro voters, jurors, or office holders. He adds that a man need not want a negro woman for a slave to refuse her for a wife. The volume preserves his 1858 words as spoken.
the-religion-of-numa-and-other-essays-on:
Jesse Benedict Carter gathers five essays on Roman religion. Macmillan issued the volume in 1906. The essays move from the religion of Numa onward. They cover the reorganization of Servius. They cover the coming of the Sibyl. A decline of faith and an Augustan renaissance close the set. The first essay argues a general rule. Rome grew by contact with the outside world.

Carter compares two ages of such contact. The republic met Greece through the Punic wars. The kings met foreign influence still earlier. That earlier wave changed the later kingdom deeply. Change through contact is his key to early Roman faith. Readers gain a clear frame for the essays. It suits anyone asking how religions absorb outside ideas.
